terms.grammar: adjective; as a noun, incommodum, incommodī n., a drawback, a disadvantage
evidence: Cic. de Or. 2.102: plūs habeat adjūmentī quam incommodī (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The noun incommodum is the negative side of a thing, set against commodum (see advantage).
Literally “turned towards, facing”; rēs adversae is misfortune, opposed to rēs secundae.

terms.gloss: that denies, negative (in logic and grammar)
terms.comment: A lawyers’ and grammarians’ word for a denying statement or particle, post-classical for negāns; it never meant unfavourable. For a negative answer, use negāre (see say).

phrases.latin: quī locus est tālis, ut plūs habeat adjūmentī quam incommodī
phrases.english: this is a point of such a kind that it brings more help than harm

phrases.latin: Habet in adversīs auxilia, quī in secundīs commodat.
phrases.english: Whoever lends in good times has help in bad times.

sources: Lewis & Short: incommodus · Lewis & Short: adverto · Lewis & Short: negativus
